title: Google Is Fighting SERP Tracking. AI Agents May Make It Worse via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
Google is entering a new phase of SERP scraping due to AI agents. Some of it may be driven by networks of LLMs that are reverse engineering Google’s search results. The public face of Google’s war against scraping remains rank trackers but the real battle may be elsewhere.
Will the ability to track rankings become a thing of the past?
What may be a reason behind Google’s actions to stop rank tracking is that the amount of AI Agent traffic has grown exponentially. According to Cloudflare, which is in a position to monitor web traffic, AI agent website traffic has increased 1,700% over the past year.
“At the end of 2024, Cloudflare handled an average of 63 million HTTP requests a second. Today, it’s almost doubled to 115 million, with peaks above 150 million. Over the past year, daily requests from AI agents on our network grew by more than 1,700%. This year, for the first time, more than half of Internet traffic wasn’t human.”
The problem with AI agent web traffic is that some of it a hybrid human/agent visit, agents working on behalf of humans, which means that some of it still has value to websites, something Google may have already considered in formulating engineering responses to rank trackers.
The problem for Google is that a massive amount of traffic could cause latency issues in serving search results, including AI search results. This is a bigger problem for keyword that trigger AI-driven search results because those are computationally more expensive to generate.
Regular search ranks pre-indexed websites that are associated with various queries. AI-derived search results include LLM inference over multiple queries, which means that every time a user asks one question, the LLM generates multiple associated queries, plus various reasoning steps, before answering with a synthesized summary of all the sources.
AI Mode is inherently more computationally expensive than traditional Search, which is why Google is aggressively reducing its AI cost per query as usage scales through improvements in LLMs, hardware and engineering optimizations.
Google’s Sundar Pichai remarked multiple times on Google’s efforts to drive the search per query costs down in the Q2 Earnings call. The cost of AI queries was so important that it merited multiple mentions:
“Yesterday we announced new models — Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite — which are cost effective and highly efficient. We’re seeing tons of demand for our workhorse Gemini Flash series, because it hits the sweet spot of performance and cost.
As we serve more of these queries, we’ve continued to drive efficiencies. Thanks to our engineering and hardware optimizations, this quarter we reduced the cost of AI Mode responses to its lowest level since launch, even as we’ve brought more advanced AI capabilities.”
The high cost per query of AI-driven Search is a real problem. AI Search queries are computationally more expensive to serve and AI agent traffic can effect search results latency. Google may very well have taken a more adversarial approach to automated rank tracking in order to improve the cost per query calculation.
Google has published multiple research papers focused on AI-generated content. The papers allude to attackers changing their content in response to Google’s reactions in order to unlock rankings. Core to unlocking rankings is tracking Google’s search results. Although the research papers don’t mention distillation, the process of reverse engineering an LLM through the outputs, the few details the research paper shares imply that is what Google is really fighting against.
Google Has Deployed A New AI Spam Detector Called SAFE
Google’s Scalable Cluster Termination System (S-CTS)
Ryan Jones ( LinkedIn profile ), developer of the SERPrecon service, extracts competitor keyword and historical search data that informs their keyword analysis for content optimization. As the principal behind this tool he is an authoritative source of information about rank tracking.
“we’re getting to the point where nobody will have rank tracking anymore because of the crazy amount of AI scraping going on.”
Jones offered the following response to someone’s tongue-in-cheek suggestion to us AI to scrape the search results (SERPs):
“that’s why the rank trackers are failing. Google is blocking all the AI trackers AND AI itself… and the rank trackers are getting caught up”
Something that has not been mentioned by Google and is not frequently discussed is that a reason why Google is discouraging rank tracking is that the data can be used to understand Google’s ranking output to build an AI Model that can reproduce Google’s search results through a process called distillation.
It may very well be that Google’s adversarial anti-rank tracking actions may be primarily an attempt to stop companies from reverse engineering Google’s search results.
Google’s decisions are made based on data and one of the problems with rank trackers is the increased cost per query. Another issue is that rank trackers distort the actual keyword inventory data. The inflation of keyword inventory is a long-running problem that predates the AI agent era, going back to the earliest days of SEO. But what’s happening today is a massive increase that quite likely distorts Google’s click and traffic metrics.
AI-driven automated crawling on behalf of humans and AI search has surged across the web. Google has to respond to automated search results scraping. Ryan Jones says the two trends are connected.

title: Holiday shopping is happening earlier than ever, here’s what brands need to know
content:
Halloween candy is still on the shelves, but holiday shoppers are making wish lists and hunting for deals months before the holidays arrive.
But as the shopping season gets longer, budgets are getting tighter. For brands, that means more chances to get in front of consumers, but also more competition for every dollar shoppers spend.
Data from Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey points to three factors that will define the holiday season: campaign timing, price sensitivity and meeting shoppers where they’re increasingly discovering gifts—on social.
Consumers have mixed feelings about how early holiday marketing should start.
According to Sprout’s Q3 2026 pulse survey, nearly half (49%) say campaigns launched as early as August make them more likely to buy, including 19% who say they’re much more likely. Just 11% say an early start makes them less likely to purchase.
But ask consumers when brands should launch their holiday campaigns and the story changes. Half point to October or November as the ideal window, compared to 21% who prefer August or September. Another 12% say brands should wait until December.
Those findings may seem contradictory, but they point to a distinction between when consumers want holiday marketing to dominate their feeds and when they’re open to discovering seasonal products. Shoppers can be receptive to gift ideas, new products and seasonal inspiration well before they want brands to go all-in on holiday messaging. In other words, an earlier presence can influence what they eventually buy without making it feel like the holiday season starts in late summer.
The sweet spot: Show up early without going all-in. Use August and September to build awareness and consideration, then ramp up your holiday campaign in October and November.
Starting earlier gives you more room to test what resonates before peak shopping begins. Then you can put more support behind the products, messages and offers gaining traction.
Brands are already putting this approach into practice. Fenty Beauty, for example, launched its limited-edition holiday collection in September, giving shoppers an early look at its seasonal products. As of writing, the TikTok has received over 100K views and over 5K likes.
Timing also depends on who you’re trying to reach. Younger consumers are especially receptive to an early start: 66% of Gen Z consumers say campaigns launching as early as August make them more likely to buy, compared to 49% of consumers overall.
Many consumers see shopping earlier as a way to get ahead of rising prices. More than a third (36%) say they’re starting their holiday shopping earlier specifically to avoid tariff-related price increases. Another 27% aren’t shopping earlier yet but are concerned about prices.
In total, 63% of holiday shoppers are thinking about the impact of higher prices.
Those concerns are also affecting how much consumers plan to spend. More than half (56%) expect to reduce their holiday spending this year because of economic conditions like tariffs and the cost of living. Only 30% say they don’t plan to cut back.
Price sensitivity doesn’t mean every brand needs to compete on having the lowest price. Shoppers may be looking more closely at what they get for their money, so holiday content should make value clear. Highlight product quality, versatility or other details that make a purchase feel worthwhile.
Discounts can also tip the scales: Promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top purchase driver, cited by 30% of consumers. Lastly, brands with products at multiple price points can also organize gift recommendations by budget, making it easier for shoppers to find options that work for them.
For example, last holiday season, REI shared a roundup of expert picks under $50 on Instagram, with a CTA to check out their larger holiday gift guide.
Social media now rivals in-store shopping for holiday gift discovery. This year, 46% of consumers say they’ll turn to social for gift ideas and product discovery—the same percentage who plan to browse physical stores.
And social’s influence is still growing. Compared to the 2025 holiday season, 28% of consumers plan to use social more to find gifts this year, while another 50% expect their usage to stay about the same.
That creates an opportunity to reach shoppers before they know exactly what they want to buy.
Think about how easily someone encountering your brand for the first time can understand what you sell, who your products are for and why they’re worth considering. Content organized around recipients, interests, occasions or price points can make that discovery process easier and give shoppers a reason to explore your products further.
Bookshop.org, for example, used Instagram to promote its 2025 holiday gift guide, which curated hundreds of recommendations for different types of readers and paired them with a limited-time discount.
Discovery is only the first step. Once shoppers find a product on social, the content surrounding it can influence whether they buy.
According to the Q3 2026 pulse survey, promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top social-specific purchase trigger at 30%, followed closely by brand posts showing products in action at 28%. Original holiday content from brands influences 26% of consumers, while 22% point to content from non-influencer users.
Taken together, these findings show that shoppers respond to a mix of incentives, brand content and recommendations from other people. Holiday content plans should reflect that variety. A steady stream of promotional posts may capture shoppers looking for deals, but product education, original seasonal content and posts from customers or creators can give others the context they need before buying.
Creator partnerships in particular can give shoppers more context as they weigh their options. In this paid TikTok partnership, creator KC walks viewers through luxury holiday gift sets, giving them a closer look at several products in one video.
Build that variety into your holiday content strategy:
Finding the perfect gift can lead to an immediate purchase—or a question about shipping, sizing or availability. This holiday season, consumers increasingly expect brands to handle both directly on social.
More than half (57%) of consumers are open to completing a purchase directly within a social app this holiday season. That includes 38% who have purchased this way before and plan to do so again, plus 19% who are ready to try it for the first time.
As more purchases happen directly on social, brands need to remove as much friction as possible. Review your social commerce strategy before holiday traffic picks up, keep product information current and make key details like availability, shipping timelines and return policies easy to find.
More than a quarter (27%) of consumers expect to use social more for holiday customer service than they did in 2025, while another 59% expect their usage to stay about the same.
Commerce and customer care increasingly overlap on social. A question about sizing, inventory or delivery might be the last thing standing between a shopper and a purchase. Plan for holiday-level service volume throughout Q4, not just during Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
Clear workflows, adequate coverage and quick access to order and product information can help social teams keep up as purchase and service activity increases.
Holiday shopping habits are changing, but the data gives marketers a clearer picture of how to adapt. As you finalize your 2026 holiday strategy, focus on three priorities:
Use these findings to benchmark your current holiday content plan and identify where you may need to adjust your timing, messaging or channel strategy. Then explore our holiday marketing strategies for more ideas to turn those priorities into campaigns that connect with shoppers this season.
When should brands start their holiday marketing campaigns?
Most consumers (50%) prefer brands to launch holiday campaigns in October or November. However, nearly half (49%) say campaigns that start as early as August make them more likely to buy. Brands can use August and September to build awareness before ramping up promotional activity in the fall.
Are consumers spending more or less on holiday shopping this year?
Consumers are planning to spend less this holiday season. More than half (56%) say they expect to reduce their holiday spending because of economic pressures like tariffs and the cost of living.
Is social media a bigger part of holiday shopping in 2026?
Yes. Social media is tied with physical stores as the top source for holiday gift ideas and product discovery, with 46% of consumers turning to each. Plus, 57% of consumers plan to complete a purchase directly within a social app this holiday season.
